name: Alexandrite laser hair removal

card.summary: A 755 nm clinic laser for hair reduction, used mainly on lighter skin with dark hair; reduction, not total removal.
card.note: Hair reduction needs multiple sessions; light, grey or red hair responds poorly, and pigment changes are a recognised risk.

quick.overview:
Alexandrite lasers emit 755 nm light that melanin absorbs strongly, so they are used for dark hair. Clinics commonly use them for fast treatment of large areas on lighter skin tones.

Published comparisons find alexandrite among the more studied hair-removal lasers. Wikipedia describes a 2006 review that found roughly 67 to 72 percent reduction at six months across alexandrite, diode and IPL.
quick.mechanism: Selective photothermolysis: the light heats melanin in hair and follicle while skin is cooled, damaging actively growing follicles. Because only growing hairs respond, multiple sessions are typically scheduled.
quick.risks: Reported effects include redness, swelling, acne flares, burns and hyper- or hypopigmentation. Lighter hair responds poorly. The FDA defines "permanent" reduction as long-term stable reduction, not guaranteed removal.

lead: Alexandrite laser hair removal uses a 755 nm laser that melanin absorbs strongly, so the light heats dark hair and its follicle and reduces regrowth. For people who want smoother, hair-free skin on the face, body or neck, or who want to stop shaving, it is one of the standard clinic options, alongside ruby, diode, Nd:YAG and intense pulsed light.[1][11] The alexandrite wavelength is often chosen for fast treatment of large areas on light to medium skin.[15]

Treatment works by selective photothermolysis: wavelength and pulse length are matched to melanin so the follicle's stem cells are damaged while surrounding skin is spared by cooling.[1] Because only follicles in the growth phase respond, most people need at least eight sessions spaced three to eight weeks apart, sometimes with touch-ups.[1] The best results are on dark hair against light skin; white, light blond, red, grey and fine vellus hair respond poorly.[1]

Studies report average hair reductions of roughly 55 to 80 percent depending on skin type and number of sessions, with pigment changes, folliculitis and blistering the main recorded complications.[13][14] The same alexandrite technology is also built into Q-switched and picosecond lasers used for tattoos and pigmented lesions, which are separate treatments.[2][3][4]

paras: Melanin in the hair is the target chromophore. Light absorbed there heats the follicle's basal stem cells, which are destroyed only if the temperature is held for long enough, so pulse duration and fluence (J/cm2) both matter, and spot size changes how deep the energy reaches.[1] Epidermal cooling by contact cooling, cryogen spray or cold air protects the skin and allows higher energy.[1] Treated hairs usually shed over two to three weeks.[1]

Alexandrite's 755 nm wavelength is absorbed by melanin more strongly than Nd:YAG's 1064 nm, which is why it is called highly effective on dark hair but also more likely to affect pigment in the skin itself.[15][11]

Wikipedia reports that hair-removal lasers were tested experimentally for about 20 years before commercial release in 1995 to 1996, following work by Anderson and Grossman on selective photothermolysis.[1] The FDA cleared the approach in 1997 for 'permanent hair reduction'.[1] A 2000 Ankara study found an alexandrite laser faster and less painful than galvanic electrolysis in 12 patients.[1] A 2005 review noted that ruby, alexandrite, diode and IPL devices all work in light skin (phototypes I to III), producing hair reduction near 75 percent, and that long-pulsed Nd:YAG is considered the safest option in dark skin.[11]

Wikipedia cites a 2006 review finding no significant short-term difference between alexandrite, diode and IPL, with about 67 to 72 percent reduction at six months, and side effects reported in 9.5 percent for alexandrite versus 28.9 percent for diode and 15.3 percent for IPL.[1]

A retrospective review of 2,359 patients in Turkey (Fitzpatrick types II to V, 3,830 sites) reported a mean 80.6 percent hair reduction six months after the last treatment, with maximum reductions of 95 percent in the underarm and 92 percent in the bikini area, and complications in 2.2 percent.[13] A trial of 144 people with Asian skin (types III to V) found 32 percent reduction at nine months after one session, 44 percent after two and 55 percent after three, supporting multiple treatments.[14] A study of a 30 mm spot-size handpiece in types II to III reported reduced hair after three to eight sessions at six-week intervals, with mean pain of 4.9 out of 10.[15]

A randomised trial of 48 axillae found hair counts fell by around 80 percent across three sessions regardless of whether treatment fell during menstruation, ovulation or the luteal phase, with pain scores lower later in the series.[12]

Itching, redness, swelling and perifollicular oedema are usually mild and last two to three days.[1] Acne flare-ups and skin discolouration are the most common serious effects; burns, hypopigmentation, scabbing, purpura and infection are also documented.[1] In the Turkish series the most frequent complications were transient hyperpigmentation (0.7 percent), folliculitis (0.5), transient hypopigmentation (0.5) and blistering (0.4), with no scarring or long-term pigment change.[13] A 1999 paper compared side effects of Q-switched Nd:YAG, long-pulsed ruby and alexandrite lasers.[5]

Wikipedia also records that large-area use of strong topical anaesthetics has caused serious harm and deaths, and that allergic reactions to gels, numbing creams or early shaving can occur.[1] Darker skin carries a higher risk of pigment change, which is why wavelength and cooling are selected by skin type.[11][14]

Laser hair removal is discussed in appearance communities as a way to clear the neck, cheeks, beard line, chest or back, and to prevent ingrown hairs; alexandrite is typically named among clinic wavelengths for lighter skin, while Nd:YAG is named for darker skin. Few forum threads in the research record address alexandrite by name.

Picosecond and Q-switched alexandrite lasers are studied for tattoos, pigmented lesions such as nevus of Ota, freckles and lentigines, and wrinkles.[2][3][4][6][7][8] A randomised trial of 755 nm laser hair removal for hidradenitis suppurativa found 75 percent clinical response on treated sides versus 33 percent on controls in a small sample.[16]

Human studies of alexandrite hair removal include a 2,359-patient retrospective series,[13] a 144-person Asian-skin trial of one, two or three sessions,[14] a randomised menstrual-cycle trial,[12] a study of a large-spot handpiece[15] and a comparison with a linear-scanning 808 nm diode laser.[17] Reviews place alexandrite among devices giving about 75 percent reduction in light skin.[11] Hair-removal side effects of alexandrite and other lasers were compared in 1999.[5] Studies of picosecond alexandrite lasers address tattoos and pigmented lesions,[2][3][6][7][8] and registered trials cover hidradenitis suppurativa and acne scars.[9][10][16]

chain: 755 nm light absorbed by melanin in dark hair
Follicle heated and damaged over repeated sessions
Fewer regrowing hairs and smoother skin
angle.text: The laser targets pigment in the hair shaft and follicle, so repeated sessions leave fewer and finer hairs on treated areas such as face, neck, chest, back, underarms or legs. It reduces regrowth rather than guaranteeing permanent removal.
